Already represented in this draft

July 29 alignment call

Included

OS 1.0 → OS 2.0, attention as focus, awareness as field, access to Self as a continuum, and the ground–core–field–focus sequence.

Source: call transcript, voicebank and approved working direction
Open full candidate material
A wider operating system

Most of us have learned to meet life through focused attention: analysing, planning, naming and solving one thing at a time. Guthrie calls this OS 1.0. It is useful, and when we rely on it alone it can become overconcentrated and effortful.

OS 2.0 adds awareness. Attention can still focus, but the focus is held inside a wider field that also includes the body, the room, other people and what matters most. Thinking is not discarded. It is transcended and included: focus stays available without having to carry the whole of experience.

The direction of the course

Participants are not asked to produce a rare or permanent state. They are helped to notice a capacity that is already present, to bring it from the background into the foreground, and to increase gradually how often access to Self appears and how long it lasts.

When access thins out, parts language offers a simple way back. “I am rushing” can become “A part of me is rushing.” The situation has not changed, but a little space may return, and from there a person can relate to the experience rather than be entirely defined by it.

Possible placement: Lesson 1 as the course frame, or Lesson 2 as the bridge from attention to awareness.

Guthrie’s presencing inductions

Partly included

The seven-minute core practice is adapted from Guthrie’s recurring live-call openings. The same source could support a short approved audio script.

Source: presencing_inductions_guthrie.md
Open full candidate material
Candidate seven-minute practice
  1. Arrive. Find an upright, comfortable position. Let the spine support you without becoming rigid. The eyes may close, or rest in a soft gaze.
  2. Ground. Feel the feet, and the weight of the body meeting the seat. Let gravity carry what it can carry. Notice any sense of stability or stillness.
  3. Core. Bring light attention to the torso: belly, chest, back and throat. Feel the body from within, without changing what you find there.
  4. Field. Let awareness open into the room: sound, peripheral vision and the body together. Thoughts and sensations can come and go inside the wider field.
  5. Focus. Let attention rest lightly on one simple thing while ground, core and field stay available. Focus does not have to collapse the wider awareness.
  6. Return. Notice how much access to Self may be present: none that you can identify, a little, or more. Finish the sentence, “Access to Self may feel like…”

This could become a Guthrie-recorded audio with transcript and captions. The final wording should keep his pacing, and needs his approval before publication.

Safety boundary for the author: every invitation is optional. If there is strain or disorientation, the instruction is to open the eyes, orient to the room and stop.

Available to add or develop

Self — ORIGINAL

Review scope

There is room here for a little more theory: Self as innate and undamaged, Self as the seat of awareness, a selection of the 8 Cs, and the markers of access. The decision to make is how much of this belongs in Week 1 without turning the week into a theory lecture.

Source: old course Week 4 handout · adapt, do not reproduce wholesale
Open full candidate material
What IFS means by Self

IFS proposes that Self is not another part, and not something a person has to manufacture. It is an innate capacity for awareness and relationship. Active protectors can obscure it; in the IFS model it is not damaged or lost.

Self can be understood as the seat of awareness: the capacity that can notice, hold and understand experience. Parts are contents of consciousness. Self is the awareness that can be in relationship with them.

How access may be recognised

The familiar eight Cs — calm, clarity, curiosity, compassion, confidence, courage, creativity and connectedness — are signals rather than a checklist to be performed. Access may also show up more quietly: a little more space, an easier breath, less urgency, softer focus, or being able to stay curious without forcing an outcome.

Self-leadership does not mean getting rid of parts. It means that parts can be seen and valued without having to run the whole system. The relationship changes first, and the experience may change later.

Week 1 could use the first two paragraphs and a short marker list. The fuller 8 Cs and Self-leadership teaching could be developed later.

The Six Organizing Principles of IFS

Review scope

The previous course’s Week 1 handout could supply one clear systems paragraph, or a visual map. It should not be compressed into the participant lesson as a protocol.

Source: old Week 1 handout in English and Russian
Open full candidate material
A light systems frame for participants
  1. We have many parts. Different inner voices, impulses and positions are a natural feature of the mind.
  2. Parts are not bad. Even when the behaviour causes difficulty, there is usually an understandable protective intention underneath.
  3. Parts live in relationship. They form patterns, react to one another, and work to keep the system safe or balanced.
  4. We are more than our parts. IFS calls the aware, relational centre of the system Self.
  5. Self is the guiding direction. More access to Self makes curiosity, clarity and compassionate leadership more available.
  6. Trust the pace of the system. Change is invited through relationship and respect, not produced by force.

For Week 1 these principles work as an orientation map. They explain why the course uses parts language, and why a participant is never asked to fight, suppress or diagnose an inner experience.

This adaptation deliberately removes practitioner instructions, client language and advanced material about exile work or unburdening.

Awareness experiments and release points

Placed by stage

The bowl-of-soup experiment belongs in the Week 1 live session, with a shared reflection afterwards. Walking and peripheral-vision practice appear only once Guthrie has introduced them. The fingers variation is held back.

Source: July 29 call exercise bank
Open full candidate material
1. Peripheral vision · after live, if introduced

Soften the eyes and notice how much of the room comes in without strain. Compare a calm moment with an ordinary busy one. The earlier fingers variation is not proposed for this course.

2. Three channels while walking · after live

Somewhere ordinary and safe, walk first with attention on seeing. Then let hearing come forward. Then let sensation in the body come forward. For the last minute, see whether all three can be present together without forcing them into equal shares.

3. The bowl-of-soup test · live session only

Imagine carrying a full bowl across a room, or run the experiment with an unbreakable cup somewhere safe. First notice what happens when attention clamps onto the object. Then find ground, widen the field, and let focus rest on the object lightly. Compare the effort, the stability and how much awareness is available.

Release rule: do not publish an experiment as independent participant practice until Guthrie has introduced it live. These are observations, not tests to pass.

Week 2 · Parts language

Parts are people, not symptoms

Included

The strongest local source for Week 2: parts as distinct inner people, with their own perspectives, needs, fears, histories, strategies and gifts.

Source: Guthrie Sayen, “Parts Are People” · previous-course lesson and Week 3 transcript · adaptation approval pending
Open adapted teaching material
Multiplicity is ordinary

A person can genuinely want to rest and genuinely want to finish the work. One part may welcome a new relationship while another is already braced for rejection. IFS treats these differences as the ordinary multiplicity of a mind, not as evidence that somebody is broken.

What makes a part more than a symptom

A part may have a characteristic age, tone, posture, body sensation, belief, hope, fear and strategy. It may still be seeing the world as it was when its role first became necessary. Meeting it as an inner person invites relationship; reducing it to “my anxiety” or “my procrastination” can hide what it is working to achieve.

Strategy and intention are different

A strategy can be costly while the intention underneath it is protective. A critic may be preventing humiliation. A perfectionist may be securing belonging. A pleasing part may be preserving attachment. An angry part may be defending a boundary, and an avoidant one may be heading off overwhelm.

Blending and unblending

When a part blends, its view can feel like the whole truth: “I am a failure”, “I have to fix this now”, “nothing matters”. Unblending does not banish the part. It makes enough room to say “a part of me believes this”, so that Self and the part can begin to know each other.

Participant boundary: use this for self-observation only. The Six Fs and the practitioner-led unblending protocol remain outside this course.

Parts form a system

Included

A light systems layer: parts react to one another, can become polarised, and may carry beliefs or emotions that are not their essential nature.

Sources: IFS Institute, “The Internal Family Systems Model Outline” and “IFS Glossary of Terms”
Open adapted teaching material
Inner sequences

Parts rarely act alone. A demanding part may push harder as a tired part withdraws; the tired part may withdraw further because it is now being attacked. Neither part is the problem by itself. The problem is the escalating relationship between them.

Polarisation

Polarised parts take up increasingly opposite positions, each because of what it fears would happen if the other won. “Work without stopping” and “refuse to begin” can both be attempts to keep the same person away from shame, failure or collapse.

Burdens

IFS uses burden for an extreme belief, emotion or role carried by a part and not understood as its essential nature. The course introduces the word so participants can follow IFS language. It does not teach an unburdening process.

Read the official model outline

Examples and reflection options

Review scope

Additional participant material for readers who want more examples without moving into practitioner technique.

Sources: old-course handout and transcript; anonymised themes from course custdev; Richard Schwartz, “Introduction to IFS” and “No Bad Parts”
Open full candidate material
A one-situation map
  1. Name one ordinary current situation.
  2. List up to three different inner positions, without deciding which is right.
  3. For each one, finish: “This part seems to want…” and “This part may fear…”
  4. Notice whether any part objects to the exercise. That objection belongs on the map too.
A language ladder

From identity towards relationship: “I am anxious” → “something in me is anxious” → “a part of me is anxious” → “I notice a part that is expecting something difficult.” Use whichever wording sounds natural in your own voice. The sentence is a way in, not a formula.

Everyday examples
  • A careful part checks the message five times so that nobody can criticise it.
  • A tired part refuses a project that a striving part has already overcommitted to.
  • A humorous part changes the subject as a conversation approaches shame.
  • An approval-seeking part says yes before anyone has checked whether there is capacity.

Optional reading: Richard Schwartz, Introduction to Internal Family Systems or No Bad Parts. Book exercises are not automatically course assignments.

Week 3 · The loving gaze of Self

Self as the seat of awareness

Included

The fuller Self teaching behind Week 3, including Guthrie’s metaphors and the distinction between Self and a Self-like part.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Self — ORIGINAL”; old Week 4 handout and live transcript; IFS Institute model outline
Open adapted teaching material
Innate rather than manufactured

In IFS, Self is not earned by behaving correctly and is not destroyed by experience. Access can be obscured while parts are carrying urgency, fear or responsibility. The underlying capacity for awareness and relationship stays where it is.

Seat of awareness

Parts are contents of consciousness: a thought, an impulse, an emotion, an image, a voice, a body pattern. Self is the capacity that can notice those contents, listen to them, and hold more than one perspective at a time.

Sun and clouds

Guthrie uses the image of the sun: clouds can obscure it without damaging it. The practice is not to attack the clouds but to recognise that the wider light is still there.

Orchestra and conductor

Self as the conductor, parts as the players. Without the conductor there may be little coordination; without the players there is no music. Self-leadership values the players and helps their different abilities serve the whole.

Eight Cs and quieter markers

Included

A richer recognition map, so that “calm” does not become a pass–fail test.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Self — ORIGINAL”; Richard Schwartz, “Evolution of the IFS Model”; Foundation for Self Leadership 8Cs resources
Open full recognition map
The familiar eight qualities
  • Calm: less internal urgency, not the absence of emotion.
  • Curiosity: real interest, rather than enquiry with an agenda.
  • Clarity: seeing more of the situation without flattening its complexity.
  • Compassion: recognising suffering without standing above it.
  • Confidence: grounded trust that does not need certainty.
  • Courage: willingness to stay present to what matters.
  • Creativity: access to more than the familiar defensive option.
  • Connectedness: contact with body, parts, people and the wider field.
Quieter signals

Other signals are quieter: an easier breath, a softer face, a lower or more open voice, less tunnel vision and more of the periphery, less attachment to one outcome, or one per cent more capacity to listen. Any of these may indicate some access to Self.

Signals of a Self-like part

A part can imitate calm while staying tight, managerial and invested in the “right” result. Where there is pressure to forgive, to perform compassion, or to make another part disappear, notice the pressure as a part rather than reading it as failure.

Force and the loving gaze

Teaching anchor

The course’s central distinction in relationship, translated into language you can observe.

Sources: Guthrie alignment calls, “BeFriending,” “Self — ORIGINAL,” and live-course language
Open comparison and practice
When force is leading

The inner language is often “get over it”, “calm down”, “explain yourself”, “change so that I can feel better”. Attention narrows, and the outcome begins to matter more than the relationship.

When more Self is available

The movement is closer to “I want to understand”, “you do not have to change for me to stay”, “what would you like me to know?” The part’s pace counts for something, and “not now” is a complete answer.

Three-breath experiment
  1. Choose a part that is present but not overwhelming.
  2. Notice how you feel towards it.
  3. If any interest or care is available, let the part receive that for three breaths.
  4. If a different reaction appears, include it and finish without forcing a resolution.

Week 4 · Protectors

Managers and firefighters

Included

A fuller non-clinical map of the two familiar protective styles, and what each may contribute once it no longer has to work in an extreme role.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Managers” and “Firefighters”; old Weeks 7–8 handouts, timelines and live transcripts
Open adapted teaching material
Managers: prevention and “never again”

Managers scan the future and try to prevent pain before it arrives. They plan, anticipate, perfect, please, criticise, achieve, control and stay alert. Because that work can look responsible and productive, people often identify with their managers as simply who they are.

A manager may carry a young, parentified logic: “I have to keep everything together, and I have to do it alone.” In a less extreme role the same part may offer organisation, discernment, care, standards and preparation — and can also step back and rest.

Firefighters: immediate relief

Firefighters respond once pain is already close. Their horizon is this moment, and their rule tends to be “whatever it takes.” Everyday strategies include scrolling, binge-watching, eating, changing the subject, joking, getting angry, cleaning instead of starting, working compulsively and going numb.

In a less extreme role, firefighters may bring rest, spontaneity, pleasure, novelty, adventure, humour and the willingness to interrupt a rigid plan.

Same aim, different timing

Managers are Plan A: prevent activation. Firefighters are Plan B: stop it or outrun it once it has arrived. Both are trying to protect the same system, even when their strategies collide.

The protection cycle

Included

A concrete system map that replaces shame about one behaviour with curiosity about the whole sequence.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Managers,” “Firefighters,” and “Exiles”; IFS Institute model outline
Open system map
  1. A manager criticises, controls or pushes in order to prevent failure or rejection.
  2. A vulnerable part feels shame, fear, loneliness or exhaustion.
  3. A firefighter distracts, numbs, escapes or erupts in order to stop the feeling.
  4. The manager reads the firefighter’s behaviour as dangerous and criticises harder.
  5. Both protectors become more extreme, because neither trusts that Self can lead.

No part in that sequence is the villain. The first useful move is usually to recognise the loop and to appreciate the intention on both sides, before trying to change any behaviour.

Use a low-intensity example such as overwork and scrolling. Avoid addiction, self-harm or severe trauma examples in participant practice.

Three messages for protectors

Included

Guthrie’s strong teaching anchor for making gratitude and permission practical rather than sentimental.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Three Messages for Protectors” and “BeFriending”; old Week 5 transcript
Open adapted teaching material
1. Validation

You have a good reason for doing this. I can see the loyalty, the work and the sacrifice in how you have been trying to help.

2. Control and permission

You can set the pace. You can say no. I will not use appreciation as a trick to get past you.

3. Hope

There may be a future in which you do not have to work this hard, and can use what you are good at in a role you would actually choose.

Questions that support relationship
  • How are you trying to help?
  • What would you like me to understand?
  • What has this role been like for you?
  • Do you ever get tired?
  • What are you afraid would happen if you stopped?

These messages only work when sincere. A protector’s “no” is information, not resistance to overcome.

Week 5 · Vulnerable parts

Vulnerability inside the system

Review scope

A humane orientation that explains vulnerability without turning the week into self-directed trauma treatment.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Exiles”; IFS Institute model outline · participant adaptation only
Open adapted teaching material
What IFS calls an exile

IFS uses exile for a young, vulnerable part whose pain, fear, shame or need has been kept out of ordinary awareness, because the system believes the feeling would be too much. In this course we usually say vulnerable part, to keep the first orientation simple.

More than the pain it carries

A vulnerable part is not only a wound. Before it took on a burden, and beneath that burden now, the part may hold openness, trust, play, imagination, sensitivity, tenderness and a capacity for intimacy.

Why protectors gather around it

Managers try to keep the vulnerable feeling from being activated. Firefighters act once it starts to break through. Respecting those protectors is part of caring for the vulnerable part, not a detour around it.

Participant learning goal: recognition and support planning. No searching for origins, witnessing procedure, retrieval or unburdening.

Recognise, orient, choose support

Core safety

The participant-facing response for when tenderness appears without warning.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “How to Handle Exiles”; old-course safety learning; IFS Institute guidance to work with protectors and negotiate pace
Open bounded response
  1. Recognise. Name that vulnerable material may be near, without deciding what it is or where it came from.
  2. Stay in the present. Feel the seat, the floor, the room. Keep your eyes open if that helps.
  3. Include protectors. Notice any wish to move away, go blank, analyse or stop. Thank it, and respect its pace.
  4. Choose, rather than continue automatically. The next step may be rest, movement, contact with someone you trust, individual therapy, or simply stopping.
  5. Escalate support when needed. Persistent flooding, disorientation, shutdown or risk calls for appropriate professional or crisis support.

The aim is not to complete an inner process. It is to stay oriented enough to make a safer choice.

Author-only safety layer

Authors only

Working material for Guthrie and the course team when deciding the demonstration, the stopping points, the referral language and the follow-up. These are design decisions for the authors, not instructions given to participants.

Sources: “How to Handle Exiles,” old Weeks 9–12 materials, participant feedback and current material rules
Open internal design guidance
  • Do not make vulnerable disclosure the price of participation.
  • Do not choose a demonstration that implies everyone should reach a young part in public.
  • Establish protector consent and a clear stop signal before any demonstration comes near tenderness.
  • Keep orientation to room, body and present support available throughout.
  • Have a named follow-up person and a referral pathway ready before the cohort begins.
  • Do not use the group to hold material that needs individual clinical support.

The archive contains practitioner steps for memory work, witnessing, retrieval and unburdening. Those steps are intentionally not reproduced here.

Week 6 · Self-led life

Self-leadership in relationship

Included

A practical relational layer for conflict, intimacy, parenting, leadership and work.

Sources: IFS Institute model outline; Toni Herbine-Blank, “Parts and Self in Relationship”; Richard Schwartz, “You Are the One You’ve Been Waiting For”
Open adapted teaching material
Internal and external systems mirror one another

How a person treats their own fear, anger or need tends to shape how they respond when those qualities show up in someone else. More compassion inwardly can make another perspective easier to hear, which is not the same as agreeing with it.

Speak for a part, not as the whole truth

“You never listen” can become “A part of me is certain I will not be heard, and it wants to push harder.” The second sentence takes responsibility and keeps the need visible.

Requests and boundaries

A Self-led request can still be firm. The difference is not softness but delivery: less threat, less diagnosis, and more clarity about what the speaker feels, needs and will do.

Repair

Parts language does not remove responsibility. A repair can name both the protector and the impact: “A defensive part took over and I spoke harshly. I understand that it hurt you. I want to come back to this differently.”

Everyday-life examples

Paraphrase only

Real applications from earlier participants, useful as recognition stories rather than as promises of outcome.

Sources: Flow 1 feedback circle, exit interviews and course custdev · direct quotation requires consent
Open anonymised examples
  • In a conflict with a partner, one participant noticed a protector, gave it room and answered later. The disagreement did not turn into a week-long fight.
  • A parent found that “a part of me is worried” took some heat out of a conversation with a teenager, where speaking as though the fear were the whole truth had not.
  • Business partners used parts language to name a perfectionistic reaction without turning the other person into the problem.
  • Participants repeatedly described Guthrie’s presence and his curious questions as part of what made more space available.

These are anonymised editorial summaries. Do not convert them into attributed testimonials until written permissions are confirmed.

Stages of familiarity

Adapted frame

A gentler version of Guthrie’s Four Stages of Competence, reframed around recognition rather than practitioner mastery.

Sources: Guthrie Sayen, “Four Stages of Competence”; circles methodology; July 29 continuation discussion
Open developmental frame
  1. I do not yet notice. A part acts, and the reaction feels like the whole of me.
  2. I notice afterwards. Reflection shows the part and the sequence once the moment has passed.
  3. I notice during. Some awareness comes back while the reaction is still happening.
  4. Relationship becomes more familiar. Parts can increasingly be noticed inside a wider field, without perfect attention being needed.

Development is uneven. Someone may have familiar access in one area of life and little access in another. Mistakes are information, not proof that the practice has failed.

Four continuation paths
  • Solo practice, for awareness and everyday parts.
  • Community or an integration circle, for continuity and shared reflection.
  • Individual therapy, when deeper or persistent material needs support.
  • Formal training, only where the goal is professional practice.

Research and claims boundary

Authors only

A factual guardrail for course and marketing language.

Source: IFS Institute Research page, accessed August 2026
Open claim guidance

The IFS Institute describes its evidence base as emerging. It points to promising pilot work and reported gains in self-compassion, and states plainly that the current literature is limited and that larger replicated trials are needed before specific clinical indications can be claimed.

  • Describe this course as education and personal development. Not treatment.
  • Do not promise trauma healing, recovery from a diagnosis, or a guaranteed therapeutic outcome.
  • Keep participant outcomes behavioural and experiential: noticing parts, creating space, using relational language, recognising when support is needed.
  • Keep evidence about clinical IFS interventions separate from claims about this six-week course.

Keep out of this participant week

Practitioner protocols and peer work

Hold back

Six Fs, triads, guiding another person, memory retrieval, exile work, unburdening and practitioner-competence framing are all intentionally excluded from this six-week participant course.

Source: old twelve-week archive · internal reference only
Open full rationale
What exists in the old archive

The previous practitioner course covered the Six Fs, practitioner–client–observer triads, guiding another person, memory retrieval, exile witnessing, unburdening, and questions of practitioner competence and supervision.

Why it is held back here

Moving that material across unchanged would alter both the audience and the level of responsibility. It could overload a foundational participant week, and it would imply peer therapy or practitioner training that this course does not provide.

What may still be translated safely

Several of the underlying principles do translate into participant language: ask permission, appreciate protective intent, respect stop signals, stay with ordinary low-intensity examples, and never force access to memories or vulnerable material.

The raw practitioner archive stays an internal reference and is not embedded in this review page.
